claim: Exact copying from context can be made much more reliable and much faster, without changing a frozen language model, by a small trained add-on that decides when the output is anchored to the source, proposes how far to copy, and accepts only the prefix of the proposed span whose source token wins by a margin after a learned per-token correction. Supported only if, for each of three backbones, it raises average exact match by at least 25% relative over normal decoding while raising throughput at least tenfold; if it beats lossless source-reuse acceleration, rule-based copy constraints and a learned pointer-style copy mechanism on average exact match; if it still adds accuracy on top of fine-tuning the model for the task; and if replacing the learned correction by fixed rules on the margin gives only marginal gains.

experiments: Build an exact-copying benchmark. Setup: four domains where one wrong character makes the output unusable: Contract (clauses requested from SEC EDGAR exhibits, 2,468 files with text, returned inside a JSON-style object with headings, numbering and subclauses intact); Literature (verbatim evidence spans such as protocols or statistical-analysis statements from 868 PubMed Central articles); Code (explain a snippet from FastAPI, SQLModel, Starlette and similar repositories, then reproduce it exactly); and Random Sequence (reproduce synthetic OpenSSH-style private keys, low-redundancy strings with line breaks and symbols). Metric: exact match of the whole target, plus decoding throughput in tokens per second; greedy decoding.

Define the add-on and its training. Setup: at each step compute the longest suffix of the output that occurs contiguously in the source (copy mode is considered only above a threshold) and the source positions that could continue it; a trigger head on the frozen model's hidden state plus this grounding length decides whether to copy; a length head predicts a tentative copy length in log space; the proposed span is replayed through the frozen model, and at each position the source token's logit margin over the best alternative is corrected by a bounded learned bias; the longest prefix with all corrected margins above zero is emitted in one step, falling back to ordinary generation otherwise. Train only the heads with a margin loss weighted toward hard near-boundary positions; base model frozen; LoRA rank 16 for the fine-tuning comparison; one RTX PRO 6000.

Compare with normal decoding and with task fine-tuning. Result (average exact match / tokens per second over four domains): Qwen3-4B 45.43 / 60.9 to 57.03 / 1,009.7; Qwen3-8B 60.28 / 55.5 to 76.97 / 842.1; Ministral-8B 49.85 / 61.6 to 76.87 / 851.1; about 15x faster on average, with gains largest on Literature and Random Sequence and smallest on Code (Qwen3-4B 54.15 to 55.02). On top of LoRA fine-tuning, average exact match rises from 82.07 to 91.35, 94.69 to 96.50 and 97.14 to 97.75, with 10-15x throughput. Differences are tested with two-tailed paired t-tests at p < 0.05.

Compare with other ways of using the source during decoding. Setup: averaged over the three backbones: lossless source-reuse acceleration (LLMA, CopySpec), a PICARD-style decoder that masks to source-consistent continuations, a rule that copies the longest matched source continuation, and a span-level pointer-generator trained on the frozen model (CopySpan). Result: lossless acceleration leaves exact match at the base level (51.85%) while speeding up to 282 tokens/s; the PICARD-style decoder (51.61%), the longest-copy rule (26.32%) and CopySpan (32.06%) are at or below the base model, the PICARD-style decoder scoring 0% on Contract because copied clauses must sit inside JSON strings; the add-on reaches 70.29% at 901 tokens/s, 3.2x and 4.7x faster than LLMA and CopySpec.

Check that the learned correction, not a margin rule, does the work. Setup: on Qwen3-8B, replace the learned bias with fixed rules (double the raw margin; add a constant 1), keeping trigger and length heads; separately ablate the length head (fixed lengths 8-256 averaged), hardness weighting and margin calibration on all three backbones. Result: on the three real domains the fixed rules give 58.11% and 59.45% average exact match against 57.97% for the base model and 72.87% with the learned correction; removing calibration drops average exact match to 44.94% / 60.47% / 50.03% (from 57.03 / 76.97 / 76.87), removing hardness weighting to 46.78% / 63.67% / 60.89%, and removing the length head mainly cuts throughput (to 299-452 tokens/s). Near-boundary analysis shows correct copy tokens have large positive margins while mismatches and overruns sit near zero.

Check robustness to prompts, sampling and domain. Setup: on Qwen3-8B with checkpoints unchanged: two paraphrased instructions and a tagged output format; temperature 0.7 with top-p 0.9 or min-p 0.05 over seeds 42-44; leave-one-domain-out training on the three real domains; 50% and 10% of the training data. Result: gains on all nine unseen prompt variants (mean +13.04 exact-match points); gains under every sampler and seed (Contract +18.7 +/- 1.5); held-out-domain training still beats the base model on average (65.53% vs 57.97% for Qwen3-8B) but trails in-domain training (72.49%), giving no gain on held-out Contract; 10% of the data keeps most of the gain (70.88% vs 76.97%).

Run inside production inference engines and check the output distribution is not distorted. Setup: Qwen3-8B in vLLM and SGLang at batch 8; compare next-token distributions of base and add-on at teacher-forced copy-exit states and sampling diversity after exit. Result: exact match 60.69% to 77.00% (vLLM) and 60.67% to 77.06% (SGLang), throughput 375 to 2,343 and 366 to 2,074 tokens/s (5.7-5.8x), heads costing under 2.7% of wall-clock; at exit states mean total-variation distance below 0.002 with no top-1 flips, and identical post-exit diversity statistics.
